extracted.intended_audience: cultivated general readers seeking guidance on manners and the qualities of a 'gentleman' (19th-century social/moral readers)
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic prescriptive account describing the qualities, manners, and social behaviors that constitute 'the gentleman' and the function of fashion and aristocracy in society. It instructs readers what traits and practices mark a true gentleman and how those differ from mere fashion or pretence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal force / original energy
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman is defined by 'original energy' and 'personal force' — a man standing in his own right who works after untaught methods and gives a sense of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'It describes a man standing in his own right and working after untaught methods.' This force enables bold action in new arenas (war → politics/trade), makes difficult things easy, and is the primary mark of leadership. Examples: Caesar, Alexander, Scipio; anti-pattern: timid talkers and clerks who lack decisive energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth / reality in conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The gentleman is 'a man of truth, lord of his own actions' — sincerity and straightforwardness in behavior are fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson emphasizes that 'the first point of courtesy must always be truth' and that good manners rest on 'reality' rather than dissimulation. Anti-pattern: skulking, dissimulation, hiding behind screens or affectations (e.g., relying on house screens rather than being present).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature / benevolence / generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Benevolence or 'good-nature' — a readiness to oblige and magnanimity — is an essential social quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'expressing all degrees of generosity, from the lowest willingness and faculty to oblige, up to the heights of magnanimity and love.' Practical result: the socially successful are 'contented and contenting' and can fill occasions appropriately (marriage, funeral, ball). Example anecdotes: Fox paying a creditor; anti-pattern: selfish, uncomfortable egotists who spoil company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste / perception of beauty / sense of measure
rubrics_metrics.description: A perception of and homage to beauty, accuracy, and proportion — 'the love of measure or proportion' — refines manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'Accuracy is essential to beauty... The love of beauty is mainly the love of measure or proportion.' Society rewards those with taste who avoid extremes and preserve balance; anti-patterns include screaming, excessive superlatives, heated conversation, and lack of proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composure / self-possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Composure, serenity, and self-content are expected: 'A gentleman makes no noise; a lady is serene.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: fashion and good-breeding require 'composure and self-content.' One should preserve the same attitude of mind in new company as daily associates, avoiding fluster, hurry, and low familiarity. Anti-pattern: noisy, hurried, or heedless behavior that offends delicate social sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference and stateliness
rubrics_metrics.description: A complementary quality to self-respect is deference — a tendency to stateliness and reserved respect toward others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'I like that every chair should be a throne, and hold a king.' He advocates coolness, absence of haste, and guarded intimacy: 'We should meet each morning as from foreign countries.' Anti-pattern: overfamiliarity that invades individual independence or breaks the island-like privacy of persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners as facilitation of fellowship
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners exist to facilitate life and fellowship: they should remove avoidable obstructions in interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson compares manners to a railway aiding travel, 'getting rid of all avoidable obstructions of the road' so people can 'energize.' Good manners are judged by whether they help or hinder social blending and conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitality / presence of a master
rubrics_metrics.description: A house must have a master: true hospitality is the presence and leadership of the host, not mere decorative trappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'No house... is good for anything without a master.' Guests seek 'Was a man in the house?' — substance and authoritative presence matter more than furniture or luxury. Anti-pattern: ostentatious homes without a guiding, present host who subordinate appendages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reliance / independence from servility
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman is not dependent or servile to persons, opinions, or possessions; he is 'lord of his own actions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson stresses independence of mind and conduct: 'not in any manner dependent and servile, either on persons, or opinions, or possessions.' True nobility is interior and not deference to external authorities; anti-pattern: deference that forfeits nobility ('any deference to some eminent man or woman... forfeits all privilege of nobility').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding pretension; authenticity over fashion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fashion and the 'false gentleman' are to be distinguished from authentic gentility: fashion may be frivolous and full of pretenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'Fashion... hates nothing so much as pretenders; to exclude and mystify pretenders... is its delight.' Yet he warns that fashion can be superficial ('a ballroom-code') and that false courtiers can exclude the true gentleman. The guidance is to value authentic generosity and character over mere fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune as ancillary, not essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth is often associated with gentility but is not essential; personal force and wide sympathy matter more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'Money is not essential, but this wide affinity is,' and he cites Diogenes and Socrates as gentlemen who chose poverty. Wealth is a natural deputy or consequence, not the defining trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellect combined with force; fine perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders require brain as well as bodily force; fine perceptions and taste are part of good breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'To the leaders of men, the brain as well as the flesh and the heart must furnish a proportion.' Defect in manners often signals defect of perception; intellectual splendor enhances society but must be tempered (not too quick/precise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in precision and punctuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not carry business-like omniscience into beautiful company; avoid excessive punctuality or precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'One may be too punctual and too precise. He must leave the omniscience of business at the door.' In social settings, excessive exactness offends; prefer tempering sharpness with gentleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy / sociability (filling the hour)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful person in society is 'happy in the company' and can 'exactly fill the hour and the company' — sociability and felicitous contribution matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson contrasts the unhappy, whose remarks are 'a little impertinent,' with the favourite, who 'finds in every turn of the conversation equally lucky occasions.' This is social tact and empathetic responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and boldness within forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Boldness that does not violate forms—'the bold fellow whose forms are not to be broken through'—is admired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson praises men who are bold yet respectful of forms: they 'give the law where he is' and 'will outpray saints... outgeneral veterans... outshine all courtesy.' Courage remains paramount even when competition shifts from war to politics/trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad affinity across classes; versatility
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman should have a wide affinity that transcends cliques and castes and can fraternize with diverse people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: the gentleman 'is good company for pirates and good with academicians' and 'makes himself felt by men of all classes.' This versatility allows leaders to be influential across society; anti-pattern: limited, clique-bound manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness balanced with originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegant manners should not be mere costume but may be original and commanding — 'not learned there, but original and commanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson notes that high behavior is rare and authentic manners can be original (e.g., a person who 'carried the holiday in his eye' and 'shook off the captivity of etiquette'), combining naturalness with courtly port when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative acts of public virtue (practical goodness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete acts of public good (rescuing the drowning, inventing charities, planting trees) signal the true gentleman and serve as centers of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson lists examples: rescuing a drowning man, planting shade-trees or orchards, guiding runaway slaves, philanthropy — these enduring, practical virtues create fashion's true sources and distinguish real noblesse from mere appearance.
